author: mpasternak
body:
Building the validator currently requires a JDK, Maven, a warm `~/.m2` cache
and a second checkout of `guidelines-cris-managers` — roughly half a gigabyte
of tooling — to produce a 4.7 MB self-contained JAR. For someone who only
wants to check their endpoint, that is the entire cost of entry.

This adds a release workflow that triggers on `v*` tags (and on demand for an
existing tag) and:

* builds with the test suite enabled, then runs the validator against the
  bundled `samples/`, exactly as `maven.yml` does;
* attaches the JAR plus a `.sha256` to the GitHub release;
* pushes the same JAR as an image to GHCR.

Nothing in the validator itself changes — no source, no tests, no `pom.xml`.
The diff is four new files.

### Two choices worth flagging

Both are easy to drop if you'd rather not have them:

* The workflow **refuses to replace the assets of an existing release**.
  `pom.xml` declares dependency version ranges (e.g. `[4.13.1,)`), which Maven
  resolves at build time, so re-running a tag can produce a different artifact
  than the one already published under it. The same reasoning is why the image
  copies the JAR from the build step instead of building its own.

* The guidelines checkout is **pinned to a tag** rather than `main`. `maven.yml`
  tracking `main` makes sense — it surfaces guideline changes early — but a
  release build wants the same schemas every time.

### Notes

GHCR is used because `GITHUB_TOKEN` already authenticates to it, so this needs
no repository secrets configured.

`NOTICE-schemas` records that the assembly embeds schemas from
`guidelines-cris-managers`, which are CC BY 4.0. They end up inside the JAR
under `schemas/original/`, and the JAR's own `META-INF/NOTICE` is the merged
NOTICE of its Java dependencies, so it does not cover them.

The `mv guidelines-cris-managers ..` step is kept rather than overriding
`-Dguidelines.project.dir`, because it turns out to be load-bearing beyond
`pom.xml`: the files in `samples/` are symlinks to
`../../guidelines-cris-managers/samples/*`, so the smoke test only works when
the guidelines repo sits next to the checkout under exactly that name.

### Disclosure

We have been running exactly this in a fork (`iplweb/openaire-cris-validator`)
since today: 43 tests plus the `samples/` check pass, and the published
artifact validates a live endpoint identically to a locally built one. If you
take this, we will drop the fork.

author: ao
body:
```wyn
impl Counter { fn bump(mut self) { self.n = self.n + 1 } }
c = Counter { n: 1 }; c.bump(); c.bump(); print(c.get())   // -> 1, want 3
```

exit 0, `wyn check` clean. The parser recorded the modifier and the checker honoured it, so nothing upstream disagreed -- only codegen did, in **three** places:

1. the impl-method **definition** emitted `Counter_bump(Counter self)`, by value. It was the only one of five parameter emitters not reading `param_mutable` (compare `codegen_stmt.c:178`, `:363`, `:3141` and `codegen_program.c:1188`);
2. its **forward declaration** had the same omission -- and a prototype that disagrees with its definition is a C error, so both had to move together;
3. the **call site** never took the address, so even with a pointer parameter the caller passed a struct. This needs to know whether the target takes `mut self`, hence the new `struct_method_takes_mut_self()`, which searches struct bodies and impl blocks the same way its sibling `lookup_struct_method_return_type()` does.

## A fourth defect surfaced while fixing it

The impl loop never called `clear_parameters()` between methods, so a `mut self` registered by one method stayed registered for the next -- making a **non-mut** `fn get(self)` emit `(*self).n` against a by-value parameter, which does not compile.

Every test case therefore pairs a mut method with a non-mut one, and two assertions exist purely to prove the non-mut path is untouched: **the fix must not quietly make every receiver a pointer**, or `self` becomes silently mutable everywhere.

## Verification

**Mutation-verified:** 7 of the new test's 11 checks fail on unfixed `dev`. The 4 that pass are the non-mut guards, which is exactly what they are for.

It also asserts on the **generated C** (definition, prototype and call site each separately), so a future change that moves only one of the three is caught by cause rather than by a wrong number. Covers int fields, string fields, extra parameters, and two mut methods in one impl block.

**Gates:** `make` 0 warnings, BDD 259/0, golden-C 30/30, examples 64/64, and all three flagship apps at baseline (wynjs 33/0 + parity 29/0, wyncanvas 26/0 + ui 171/0, VisualWyn 15/0, wynstorm 32/0). Re-run after rebasing onto the merged `dev`.

body:
Fixes #29904

## Description
In `packages/platform/types/event-types/event-types_2024_06_14/outputs/booking-fields.output.ts`, default booking field output classes (`NameDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `EmailDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `LocationDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `NotesDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `GuestsDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `TitleDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `RescheduleReasonDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `PhoneDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`, `SplitNameDefaultFieldOutput_2024_06_14`) declared `@DocsProperty` on `isDefault = true` without explicit `type: Boolean` metadata.

In Swagger/OpenAPI reflection, initialized properties on derived output classes without explicit type metadata get inferred as `type: object`, causing generated OpenAPI documents to declare `isDefault` as `type: object` while emitting boolean default values.

This PR explicitly adds `type: Boolean` to `@DocsProperty` for `isDefault` across default and custom booking field output schema definitions, ensuring OpenAPI generators correctly emit `type: "boolean"` in schema output.

body:
The wheel shrank from 42rem to 28rem in #791, but the panels beside it didn't follow. eveship.fit authors `ShipStatistics` and `HardwareListing` in fixed px — the stats panel is a hard `width: 350px` — so unlike the wheel they follow neither a font-size nor a container width, and the capacitor/EHP/DPS numbers stayed full size next to a two-thirds wheel.

Both now shrink by the same factor. `.layout` declares one `--fit-scale` knob and the panels apply it with `zoom`, which scales the used layout box along with the contents, so the column beside the wheel really is the width it looks (a transform would leave a full-size hole in the flex row). Modules move onto the wheel by native HTML5 drag-and-drop through `dataTransfer` with no coordinate math, so zooming a drag source doesn't disturb dropping.

The "Load modules & ammo" browser moves out from under the wheel into a column to its **left**, the way EVE's fitting window arranges it, scaled to match and open by default now that it no longer dominates the page. It's last in the DOM and ordered left by CSS, so below the width where three columns fit it stacks at the bottom rather than above the ship. Its listing is sized so it renders exactly as tall as the wheel is wide. `fitPlaceholder.tsx` holds all three columns so the viewer's arrival still fills a reserved box.

The heading is now a shared `ShipHeading` (used by both the signed-in and share-link views): the hull's 64px `render` to the left of the name, with the owner under it at 17px carrying the pilot's portrait or the corporation's logo. `TypeIcon` grew a fetch-size ladder so a 64px icon isn't a 64px image stretched, and takes a `className` for icons that aren't its inline-beside-a-name default.

## Testing

- `pnpm run lint`, `pnpm run build`, `pnpm test` (115 pass) all clean.
- Layout geometry checked in headless Chromium against a harness replicating the copied CSS with px stand-ins for the eveship.fit components: at 1280px the browser is 256px wide on the left, the wheel 448px, the stats panel 233px (350 × 0.667) on the right, and the listing renders 448px tall — matching the wheel. author: samli-jolli
body:
## Problem

Both plugin READMEs are published to more than one marketplace, but each carried a single hardcoded install target. Dev and prod use the **same repository name in two different orgs**, so the dev mirror told dry-run readers to add the *public release* repo instead of the rehearsal copy.

## Change

The source READMEs now keep a neutral `<marketplace-source>` placeholder wherever they name the marketplace to add, and a new `publish_readme_source` helper resolves it on the **mirrored copy**:

| Target | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `publish-prod.sh` | the public org slug |
| `publish-dev.sh` | the dev org slug |
| `publish-local.sh` | the local directory it just wrote |
| `publish-zip.sh` | a generic absolute path (recipient picks where they unzip) |

Resolution runs after `publish_sync` (which would overwrite it) and before the commit. The slug is **passed in** by each publish script rather than derived from the checkout's `origin`: the README is written before the push, so a mistyped destination should not silently produce a README documenting whichever repo that checkout happens to point at.

Publishing **fails loudly** when the placeholder is missing. `README.md` is not covered by the dist or config inventories, so nothing else would notice a README edit that drops or renames the token — and shipping the literal token is an install command that cannot work. Replacement uses `awk` substr arithmetic rather than `sed`, because slugs and absolute paths contain both `/` (delimiter) and `&` (backreference); since that rewrites at most once per line, the helper then asserts the token is gone.

## Front door

Both READMEs now point at the bare `/jolli` (`$jolli` on Codex) front door instead of `jolli:init`. The umbrella reads how the repo is set up and routes into init itself when setup is incomplete, so naming the sub-skill first skipped the state-aware entry point.

- The Claude README keeps the first-session caveat — its umbrella is a project skill the plugin *writes*, not a bundled one, so a brand-new repo may not show it until the next session.
- The Codex README drops its Development section: the published repo is a generated release artifact, and its readers should be sent to the monorepo for source, issues, and patches.

## Tests

Shape tests pin both halves, which live in different files and are not type-checked — the placeholder's presence and its one-per-line form, and each script's own slug. New `ClaudePluginPublishDocs.test.ts` mirrors the technique already used for Codex in `CodexPluginManifest.test.ts`.

`npm run all` passes: all four build targets, both typechecks and lints, CLI 372 files / 10136 tests, 5 acceptance files, vscode 109 files / 4536 tests.

Follow-up to #155204 (was a `TODO` in `RecoveryDirectCancellationService`).

The snapshot path always reads the latest cluster state, but every `clusterChanged` with `WAITING` shards queued its own generic-thread run. Extra runs were mostly harmless, later deduplicated by the send cache, but still wasted master work under rapid routing or snapshot updates.

This PR coalesces those runs:

- `pendingSnapshotCancellationRun` keeps at most one snapshot-cancellation task queued. It is cleared at the start of each run so a concurrent trigger can schedule a follow-up against a fresher state.
- Extracted `CancelUndesiredRecoveriesRunnable` / `CancelRecoveriesBlockingSnapshotRunnable` for readability, desired-balance behavior is unchanged. `CancelRecoveriesBlockingSnapshotRunnable#doRun` is `synchronized`, to delay the next run until the previous one is finished.

author: t0msilver
body:
## Problem

In section 3.2 (the sensitivity panel), the dashed nearest-flip tick did not land where the bar changes colour, nor where the red underline starts — the very transitions the caption says it marks.

Verified with Playwright by dumping the rendered SVG geometry: the tick was consistently offset by exactly **half a sweep-grid stride**, e.g. warm-turn-size row ~20 px right of the boundary, speculative-speedup row ~16 px left of it (direction follows the outward scan direction). Invisible on the dense 41-point axes, obvious on the coarse 13–17-point workload axes.

## Cause

Two renderers used different conventions for where a transition "is":
- the colour bands and the does-not-fit underline place segment edges at the **midpoint between adjacent sweep samples**;
- the tick was drawn at the **first sample past the flip** found by the outward scan in `computeFlipData`.

## Fix

Record the neighbouring sample in the flip object and draw the tick at the same inter-sample midpoint the bands use. The right-hand label keeps citing the sampled flip value, which stays truthful (the first sampled value where the change holds).

After the fix, all seven rows' ticks sit at 0.00 px from their band/underline edge (checked programmatically from the rendered SVG).

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Warm turn size | tick ~20 px right of the flip | on the boundary |
| Speculative speedup | tick ~16 px left of the handover | on the boundary |

author: vanyastaff
body:
Closes #976.

## The problem

`Orchestrator::handle_entry` awaits `sink.dispatch(&msg)` — a whole execution step that, by its own comment, "can park on a durable timer or an external wait" — and only then calls `mark_dispatched`. The dispatch claim is therefore held for the entire action duration, which makes the queue's reclaim timeout an implicit limit on how long an action may run. A slow action outlives its claim, a sweep redelivers the row, and a second worker starts a turn the first is still running.

Renewing the claim while the action runs does not fix it: it turns the queue row into a second, weaker lease competing with the execution aggregate's own.

## The shape

`ExecutionTurnHandoff::accept_turn` ends the claim at a definite point. It acquires the execution lease under the aggregate fence **and** acknowledges the queue row in one transaction, so the two can never disagree:

- Crash before the commit — the row is still `Processing`, the sweep redelivers, and no turn was accepted.
- Crash after — the row is acknowledged and the execution holds a durable lease, so recovery drives from aggregate truth rather than from the queue.

The trait doc explicitly forbids assembling this from `acquire_lease` + `mark_dispatched`: those are separate operations, and the crash window between them is the state this capability exists to make unreachable.

`TurnHeldByAnotherOwner` deliberately leaves the queue row unacknowledged. Acknowledging there would drop the turn on the floor — the row would be terminal while no owner ever ran it — so it stays claimable and the sweep redelivers once the competing lease expires.

The handoff carries a `JobClaimToken`, not a processor identity: a stable processor may claim a row, lose it to a sweep, and claim it again, so an acknowledgement issued against the first claim would terminalise a row the second is still working.

## Backends

SQLite takes the write lock up front with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. PostgreSQL re-reads the claim row `FOR UPDATE`, closing the window where a reclaim sweep could move it between the check and the acknowledgement. Both stamp the lease deadline in the database, matching `acquire_lease` — a caller's clock never decides liveness, because one running fast would fence out a healthy peer and one running slow would mint an already-dead lease, neither detectable from the row afterwards.

When the lease cannot be taken, one extra read distinguishes a live foreign lease from a missing execution: a caller must not treat a nonexistent execution as contention it can wait out.

## Two findings from writing the evidence

Both recorded rather than smoothed over:

- **`SELECT 1` is INT4 in PostgreSQL, not INT8.** Decoding the existence probes as `i64` failed at the driver. Only the live-PostgreSQL run could surface this; a SQLite-only suite would have shipped it.
- **The reclaim predicates disagree at the boundary.** The in-memory model uses `elapsed >= reclaim_after`, SQLite uses `processed_at_ms < cutoff`, so a zero window reclaims immediately on one backend and never on the other. The SQL cases backdate the claim explicitly rather than depend on either reading. The divergence is pre-existing reclaim behaviour, named here so it is not rediscovered later as a flake.

## Scope note

This PR lands the storage capability and its three-backend evidence. The orchestrator refactor to `claim → validate → handoff → dispatch` follows on this branch; the acceptance criterion about a blocked action outliving its claim is proven end-to-end there.

- 6771 workspace tests pass (3 skipped); 598 nebula-storage tests.

- The PostgreSQL suite is added to the required `postgres-conformance` job rather than left to skip.
- clippy clean on default, sqlite-only, postgres-only, and all-features; `task quality` green.

body:
Follow-up to **#421** — acting on the Codex review [4863369036](https://github.com/xAlisher/peers/pull/421#pullrequestreview-4863369036). #421 was already merged and its branch deleted, so the fix lands here instead of on that branch.

## The finding (confirmed)

> Adding this flag is not enough to make cancellation cancel the send. `sendStagedVideo` unconditionally calls `Storage.uploadEncrypted(enc.path, id)` after `transcode()` resolves; on the cancellation path that `path` is explicitly the original video.

Verified against the code. `VideoTranscoder.transcode()` resolves a cancelled job with `{skipped:true, cancelled:true, path:<original>}` — the **same `path` shape** as the graceful "compression failed, send it anyway" fallback. `sendStagedVideo` only read `path`, so it fell through to `uploadEncrypted` + `send()` and shipped the untouched original — exactly the video the cancel targeted. `cancelTranscode()` cancelled the *encode* but not the *send*.

## Change

One guard in `sendStagedVideo` before the upload: on `enc.cancelled`, clear the in-flight `mediaSends` bubble and return. `skipped` **without** `cancelled` still sends, unchanged — a failed compression is not a cancel.

## Tests

`__tests__/videoCancel.test.ts` — 5 cases, registered in the `jest.logic.config.js` `testMatch` allowlist:
- cancelled ⇒ no `uploadEncrypted`, no `send`
- cancelled ⇒ bubble cleared, **no** error surfaced (a cancel is not a failure)
- cancelled ⇒ never stuck in the `sending` phase
- normal compress ⇒ still uploads the encoded path + sends
- `skipped` but not cancelled ⇒ still sends the original

The two cancel assertions **fail on the pre-fix code** (verified by reverting the guard) and pass with it.

## Gate

- `npx tsc --noEmit` → clean
- `npx jest --config jest.logic.config.js` → **318/318** (was 313; +5)
- `assembleRelease -x lint` → BUILD SUCCESSFUL

## On-device

Installed to RedMe + Samsung; a real video send (pick → compress → upload → send) completed with no FATAL / signal 11 on either. **The cancel path itself was not exercised on device** — nothing in the UI calls `cancelTranscode()` yet (#421 listed the bubble cancel affordance as a follow-up), so it is covered by unit tests only. ## Summary

The publish dispatch failed on the first release that ever reached it. `v0.1.8` was tagged and released on GitHub, then the step that hands off to `publish.yml` died with:

```
failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
```

The `release-please` job never checks the repo out, so `gh` had no git remote to infer the repository from, and it exited before dispatching anything. GitHub said 0.1.8 was released while npm stayed on 0.1.7.

## Changes

- `gh workflow run publish.yml` now passes `--repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"`, so the step takes the repository from the runner's environment instead of a checkout it does not do.
- A two-line comment says why the flag is load-bearing, since it looks redundant to anyone who assumes the job has a working tree.

## Testing

0.1.8 was published by a manual dispatch, run 30998514271, which went green on the `workflow_dispatch` event and put 0.1.8 on npm. That proves the receiving end works and isolates the failure to the dispatch call itself.

This change cannot be proven until the next release cuts unattended. Nothing about it is testable in CI: the step only runs when `release_created` is true. The next `fix:` or `feat:` merged to main is the real test, and the fallback stays what it was, dispatch `publish.yml` by hand against the tag.

`ci:` is hidden in the changelog, so this cuts no release on its own.

## Vulnerability

A crafted `SAMLResponse` carrying **two assertions** was accepted as authentic:

1. a forged, **unsigned** assertion holding the attacker's attributes, followed by
2. a genuine, **signed** assertion issued by a real Identity Provider.

The signature check found the single signature (on the second assertion) and validated it, while both the security checks in `Response::validate()` and the attribute extraction in `spidSession()` read the **first** assertion via `getElementsByTagName(...)->item(0)`. The element the library authenticated was therefore not the element it read the identity from: a classic SAML **signature wrapping (XSW)** attack allowing full impersonation of any user (**CWE-347**, **CWE-349**, **CWE-290**). The `spid-drupal-module` inherits the flaw and turns it into privilege escalation to administrator.

This was reported in a security bulletin covering `spid-php-lib` and dependent projects.

## Fix

Response validation is hardened in three layers so that the element the library reads is provably the element that was cryptographically validated:

- **`BaseResponse::validate()`** rejects any response that contains more than one `Assertion` or more than one protocol root, rejects a `Signature` placed anywhere other than the assertion or the root (and a second signature on the same element), and — as defence in depth — rejects any response in which an identity-bearing element (`NameID`, `Conditions`, `Audience`, `AttributeStatement`, `AttributeValue`, `AuthnContextClassRef`, …) appears **outside** the signed assertion. The counts mirror the namespace-agnostic `getElementsByTagName()` the downstream code uses, so a forged copy in a foreign namespace cannot slip through either.

- **`SignatureUtils::validateXmlSignature()`** now copies the signed element (and only that element) into an isolated document before verifying, instead of cloning the whole document and locating the *first* signature. It also confirms the enclosing element is actually among the nodes the reference digest covered, so a signature whose `Reference` points at a wrapped child cannot be passed off as covering its parent.

## Tests

`tests/SignatureWrappingTest.php` builds a genuinely signed response and the attack variants:

- ✅ genuine signed response is accepted and the session carries the **signed** assertion's attributes (no regression);
- ✅ forged unsigned assertion placed before the signed one → rejected, no session created;
- ✅ forged `AttributeStatement` at response level, outside the assertion → rejected;
- ✅ tampered signed assertion → rejected;
- ✅ assertion signed by an untrusted key → rejected.

## Verification

Full pipeline (`composer validate`, `phpcs --standard=PSR2`, `phpunit`) run in `php:X-cli` containers on **7.4, 8.0, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, 8.5** — 41 tests, 109 assertions, green on every version.

Supersedes the partial mitigation in #153 (thanks @VinsMach): that PR rejected multiple assertions and isolated the signed subtree; this PR keeps both ideas and adds the reference-coverage check and the "no identity element outside the signed assertion" defence, with regression tests.

## Summary

Fixes empty ESM main-entry emission under Vite 8 / Rolldown when `vite:esm-shim` injects the CJS shim after a false “static import” match inside string/template payload.

### What changed

- **`vite:esm-shim`**: mask string, template, and comment spans (same length → original indexes stay valid) before:
  - detecting CJS syntax (`__dirname` / `require(…)`), and
  - finding the last static `import` for shim insertion
- **`swcPlugin`**: set `oxc: false` alongside `esbuild: false` so Vite 8 does not ignore the disable and warn that only Oxc must be turned off

### Why

Large main bundles often embed schema/SQL/source text such as:

```ts
import {XxxModel, XxxOption} from './XxxModel.js';
```

The previous regex scanned the raw rendered chunk, treated those as real top-level imports, and injected the shim mid-string → corrupted chunk → Rolldown could emit `dist/main/index.js` as **0.00 kB**.

Reported detail and instrumentation in #906. #916 is the Vite 8 SWC transform warning.

Separately, localm/plugins/gui/web.py's upload-delete route resolved a caller-supplied name directly against an existing file with no protection against an OS-level short-name alias resolving to a different, pre-existing file - the one place in that file without the non-clobbering retry-with-counter the write path already has. Fixed by routing it through the hardened, shared confined_name, which rejects an alias as a side effect of its existing strict name-match check.

Verified: the full existing pathsafe/web.py/upload/share test suites pass unchanged across every current caller (524 tests). New regression tests use the same live monkeypatch technique #1068's own tests established. author: ecfromthedc
body:
## What this is

The operator-experience half of the dogfood build, plus four defects found by
auditing this tree the way an outside reviewer would.

Every item below is: **in the tree · gated · mutant-proved · registered in
`test/suite-baseline.txt` · committed.** A mutation that does not APPLY is
INCONCLUSIVE, never a pass — one suite's mutant stopped applying during this work
and the gate correctly went RED rather than passing silently.

## New capability

**Sub-agents can spawn sub-agents, under contract.**
`stitchpad spawn <name> --brief <text> --artifact <path>...`

Spawning is the easy half. The contract is the point: an unconstrained spawn
recreates, one level down, the most expensive defect of this build — a seat that
produces nothing looking exactly like a seat that is working.

- `--artifact` is **mandatory**; an unscoreable seat cannot be created.
- Lineage is durable, so a silent seat is attributable to whoever asked for it.
- Depth and fan-out are bounded. An agent that can spawn agents can fork-bomb the
  operator's laptop.
- Cycles and anonymous spawns are refused, and every refusal names the fix.
- Dispatch **reuses** the mention → watcher → `fire_adapter` path — the one proven
  to deliver. This command must never grow a second private dispatch path.

`stitchpad directive <text>` records the orchestrator's standing order, copied
**verbatim** into every spawn brief at every depth and marked as outranking the
parent's brief. That is what "always follow the orchestrator's request" is made
of: depth cannot dilute the original ask.

## Defects fixed

**`wake` silently swallowed push-seat messages.** Measured on the live pad: an
orchestrator ran `stitchpad wake kimi`; the command rendered the message to the
*orchestrator's* terminal, advanced `seen.kimi` to 5, and exited 0 — while the
daemon showed no turn on that session since the previous day. The cursor had
moved, so it was never retried. It looks exactly like success. Now refused,
cursor untouched, with the working command named. Self-wake and `--peek` are
unaffected.

**The live roster dropped every operator.** `join --role operator` writes
`.state/role.<name>`; `sp_roster_live` read `.state/runtime.<name>`, which nothing
in the tree writes. Its own comment promised operators are "always kept". They
were not — they fell through to a heartbeat check they have no heartbeat for.
Both halves look correct in isolation and nothing errors.

**A push seat could not be enrolled from an occupied terminal.** ONE TERMINAL =
ONE PAD is for seats that *occupy* a terminal; a push seat is daemon-driven. Pull
seats are unchanged and still refused — asserted explicitly, because that is the
security half.

**The release gate scored crashes GREEN.** Crash detection matched an *enumerated*
list of bash messages, so a suite dying on `x=$((1/0))` printed a diagnostic,
continued with a wrong value and exited 0. Now matches the bash fatal-diagnostic
*shape*, which catches every message nobody thought to enumerate. Separately, the
VOID path printed `TRIPWIRE: PASSED` and then exited 2; a run that could not be
measured is not a pass, and now says so.

**An empty artifact counted as produced.** Proved live: a dispatched seat wrote
the stub header it was told to create first, did no work, returned rc=0, and the
board scored it present. Empty files and empty directories no longer count, and
the duplicate presence test in the lanes sidebar now routes through one oracle.

## Documented, not fixed (daemon-side)

**P45 — a dispatched agent's turn is not observable.** The turn record is
`id, session_id, prompt, status, started_at, finished_at` — there is no output
field, `finished_at` equals `started_at` to the millisecond while the agent is
still working, and `/messages` returns 405. An orchestrator cannot read one word
an agent said, and `rc=0` means "the turn was delivered", never "the work
happened". Ruled out by execution: not dispatch (a two-step probe ran both
steps), not permissions, not prompt visibility. The fix belongs in Ocean. Until
then the artifact contract is the only observable an orchestrator controls, which
is why it is now mandatory rather than advisory.

## Coverage

New gates: `p42-subagent-spawn-gate.sh` (12), `p43-wake-push-misdirect-gate.sh`
(7), `p44-roster-live-role-key-gate.sh` (7).
`artifact-contract-gate.sh` 13 → 18. All registered and mutant-proved.

One gate caught **itself** lying: its fixture joined a second pull seat, which
ONE TERMINAL = ONE PAD correctly refuses, so the seat was never in the roster and
the assertion was vacuous. It now asserts the fixture exists before claiming
anything about it.

## Two more, found by running the gate rather than reading the code

**`stitchpad help` hid six commands.** It printed a hardcoded line range
(`sed -n '2,44p'`), while the header block runs to line 57. Four commands had
already fallen off the end unnoticed — `reconcile`, `lanes`, `pads`, `evidence` —
and the two new ones joined them. The discoverability gate never caught it because
it read the header directly and never compared it to what `help` actually prints.
Help is now self-maintaining, and the gate compares the two surfaces.

**`test-runner.sh` ran against a half-built sandbox.** It copied `stitchpad` and
`lib.sh` but not `date-divider.sh` or `session-registry.sh`, which `stitchpad`
sources at startup. Every invocation printed two bash "No such file or directory"
diagnostics and ran against a broken tool — and the suite still printed
"test runner ok" and exited 0. It scored GREEN until crash detection started
matching the diagnostic *shape*.

## Where I got it wrong, recorded because it matters

The widened crash detector produced a **false positive** on its first outing:
`watcher-races.sh` kills a background job it started, and bash reports that as
`<script>: line 103: 46691 Killed: 9 …` — the same shape as a fatal diagnostic.
My first fix enumerated the status words, which is the very mistake shape-matching
exists to avoid, and a run under load produced a word not on the list. The
structural rule needs no list: a job-status line carries a bare PID right after
`line N:`. Crash-shaped statuses are re-admitted explicitly. Both greps end in
`|| true`, because a grep matching nothing exits 1 and under `set -e` that killed
the classifier and turned 21 of the gate's own assertions red.

I also spent a long stretch bisecting `operator-conduct-gate.sh` as a regression of
mine. It was not. It is load-sensitive, and I was running several tripwires and
agent dispatches concurrently. An interleaved A/B with the machine quiet gave 8/8
on both trees three times running. The lesson is the one already written into this
build after P39: **measure the base rate before treating a failure as a signal.**

## Open, documented, not fixed

**P45** — a dispatched agent's turn is not observable (daemon-side).
**P46** — dispatch is one-shot with no feedback loop. Three review seats (k3 and
two DeepSeek) were dispatched against this tree; all three returned rc=0 having
written only their stub headers. A k3 seat given four *specific* claims to verify
still produced only a scaffold, so the limit is not prompt breadth: a wake turn
executes a short explicit sequence and does not sustain open-ended investigation.
What is ours to fix is that nobody verifies the contract when a turn ends and
nobody tells the agent it is not finished. The proposed fix — contract-driven
supervision that re-wakes the same session with a small delta until the artifact
exists — is specified in the ledger.

## Gate

`TRIPWIRE: PASSED — all 76 enforced suites green` (exit 0), run with the machine
quiet. New suites registered and mutant-proved: `p42-subagent-spawn-gate.sh` (12),
`p43-wake-push-misdirect-gate.sh` (7), `p44-roster-live-role-key-gate.sh` (7).
Updated: `artifact-contract-gate.sh` 13→18, `help-discoverability-gate.sh` 86→91,
`command-dispatch-gate.sh` 72→79, `tripwire-gate.sh` 28→34.

body:
## ELI-5 You ask the assistant to restart ComfyUI. It stops the one it started — except it never started one, because *you* opened ComfyUI yourself. So it tries to start a fresh one, and the port is already taken by your ComfyUI. Until now it could only shrug: "something is on this port, probably not mine, go kill it yourself." Now it looks. It asks comfy-cli "what is on port 8188, and would you stop it?", comfy-cli answers with the actual process — pid, command line, port — and you get asked: *stop THAT and restart?* Say yes and it does. Say no and nothing happens, except the error you get now names the exact process instead of guessing at it. ## Summary Implements option C of the untracked-server spike: compose comfy-cli's verified stop behind per-call consent, rather than leave `restart_comfyui` unable to recycle the server the user pointed it at. When `_restart_comfyui_locked` hits its existing signature (nothing recorded to stop **and** the launch lost the port), it runs `comfy stop --port

--dry-run` inside the already-held lifecycle slot. If comfy-cli positively identifies a ComfyUI, the user is asked via elicitation — the prompt names the **pid, command line and port** — and on approval `comfy stop --port

` runs and the launch is retried **once**. Declining, an unverified listener, and a comfy-cli that predates `comfy stop --port` all land on today's `_untracked_server_guidance` error, enriched with the dry-run identity when there is one. The two honesty deltas the spike named are closed on the identified path: the message names a PID, and it drops the "almost certainly started outside comfy-cli" hedge — which stays, correctly, on the path where nothing was identified. ## Changes - `_verified_untracked_listener(port)` — thin read of `comfy stop --port

--dry-run`. Returns `None` on any failure, which is also the **capability probe**: a comfy-cli without the flag rejects it while parsing, that arrives as a `ComfyCliError` like any other refusal, and the caller falls back to the error it always raised. No version comparison, no special case. A payload that does not positively assert both `verified` and `dry_run` is treated as no answer. - `_KILL_UNTRACKED_APPROVAL_WORDING` + `KillUntrackedApproval` over the shared `_elicit_approval` body, per the AGENTS.md rule that a new gate brings wording, not a second copy of the handling. `_kill_untracked_wording(port)` fills the escape hatch with the real port so it names `comfy stop --port 8188`, not a placeholder. - `_resolve_kill_untracked_consent` keeps `_resolve_switch_consent`'s two properties: **elicitation wins even when `confirm_kill_untracked=True`**, and an **unknown client capability counts as capable**. What it does *not* keep is the raise — `_elicit_approval`'s fail-closed errors (unanswered prompt, client that errored) fold into the refusal reason so every "no" surfaces as one enriched error rather than three shapes. - `_kill_consent_from_thread` bridges the worker thread back to the event loop. The clash is only discoverable *after* the stop half, the sequence holds `_lifecycle_slot` (a per-thread reentrant lock), and hopping back to the loop to ask would mean dropping that slot mid-sequence — exactly the gap a concurrent `stop_comfyui` slips into. So the worker keeps the slot and blocks while the loop, idle awaiting this very `to_thread`, raises the prompt. - New tool param `confirm_kill_untracked: bool = False` — the prompt-incapable-client fallback, pointing at `comfy stop --port

` in a terminal. - `_kill_target_port` separates "no `--port` was passed" (falls back to 8188) from "`--port` was passed and could not be read" (no kill offered) — `_requested_port` answers `None` to both, and guessing 8188 for the second would show a process on a port the caller never asked about. - `stop_comfyui` the tool is untouched: still ownership-only, so the kill is reachable only through restart's gate — one consent chokepoint. - `AGENTS.md` + the `README` tool table updated in the same PR, per the keep-in-sync rule. ## Motivation The spike found the "precise error" half had already shipped, leaving a purely behavioral gap: `restart_comfyui` still could not recycle the server it was pointed at, and the static refusal routed the user to a **blunter** manual action (`kill` in a shell, verifying nothing). A consent prompt naming the exact process comfy-cli itself vouched for is the stronger safety property — and after this, the *refusal* names it too. ## Testing - [x] Existing tests pass (`pytest` — 1835 passed, 4 skipped) - [x] Lint passes (`ruff check .`) - [x] Format check passes (`ruff format --check .`) - [ ] Tested manually — **not possible here**: `comfy` is not installed in this environment (`which comfy` → not found), so no live end-to-end run against a real untracked ComfyUI. See the falsification note below for what was verified instead. New file `tests/test_untracked_kill.py` (46 tests) covers: approve → kill then launch retried once; decline / cancel / accept-without-yes / unanswered prompt / client that errors → no kill and the enriched error; dry-run unverified, dry-run refused (`unverified_process`, `port_not_listening`), a comfy-cli that rejects `--port`, and every malformed payload shape → **no prompt at all**; `COMFYUI_URL` / `COMFYUI_HOST` sessions (including a malformed one) → neither probe nor prompt; `confirm_kill_untracked=True` does not bypass a prompt the client can show; an unreadable capability probe still asks; a failed kill does not go on to relaunch; a failed relaunch says the server WAS stopped; and the argv the probe spawns. One hermeticity fix in `tests/test_wrapper.py`: its port-clash guidance tests reach this branch while patching only `stop_comfyui` / `_launch_comfyui_sync`, so without a stub the new probe would spawn a **real** `comfy` child on any machine with comfy-cli installed. An autouse fixture pins it to "comfy-cli would not vouch", which is the state those tests are about anyway. ## Additional Notes **Negative-claim falsification.** This change's user-facing outcome is mostly the *opposite* of a denial — it adds a route where there was none, and the refusal paths it keeps are the pre-existing error, not a new dead-end. The one premise that needed checking is the engine contract it composes, and it was verified against merged source rather than assumed: `comfy stop --port

[--dry-run]` exists on `Comfy-Org/comfy-cli` `main` (commit `505cf8a`, PR #675 — the blocker this ticket named). The payload this PR consumes matches `comfy_cli/schemas/stop.json` field for field (`stopped` / `dry_run` / `verified` / `untracked` / `pid` / `port` / `cmdline` / `cwd`), and the refusal codes it degrades on are that commit's own `port_not_listening` and `unverified_process`. The dry-run branch emits with `changed=False` and does not kill, and the real stop re-finds and re-verifies the listener before killing. I could not execute the binary here (not installed), so the live end-to-end run is the one unverified step. **Judgment calls, flagged for review:** 1. **Remote sessions skip the kill path**, per the ticket's test list. Worth naming the tension: `comfy stop --port` is local-only regardless of `COMFYUI_URL` (it walks the local process table), so this skip is *conservatism*, not a correctness requirement — with a remote configured, which machine's port is in question stops being obvious, and "obvious" felt like the right bar for killing a process. A malformed `COMFYUI_URL` reads as "configured", never as "local". Easy to relax later if you'd rather it fire. 2. **The prompt is raised from the worker thread** (`asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe`) instead of unwinding to the event loop. This is the riskiest line in the diff. It is safe because the loop is idle — it is awaiting this exact `to_thread` — and the wait is bounded twice (`_ELICIT_TIMEOUT` inside the prompt, `_KILL_CONSENT_WAIT` outside it), with every failure a refusal. author: hughgrigg
body:
`splitWadeGiles` and `readWadeGilesWord`, which is the first half of what
Phase 6 had left. Wade-Giles hyphenates its syllables and the hyphen is
not decoration — the system has no 隔音符号 to fall back on, because its
apostrophe marks aspiration instead — so a text that dropped it has
thrown away the only boundary marker there was.

**Measured before it was built, and the two questions turned out to have
opposite answers.** ROADMAP.md recorded this as one hard problem
multiplying against the 52.07% of written syllables that lose their
identity when the marks come off. It is two problems, and only one of
them is hard. Over the same 411,956 multi-syllable words of the phrase
corpus that figure comes from, written in Wade-Giles and run together:

| | marks kept | marks dropped |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the boundary is found | 99.19% | 99.04% |
| the word comes back | **99.45%** | **56.04%** |

The boundary is found either way. What collapses is the *reading*, and
only once the marks are gone — which is the ambiguity this module already
measures, arriving a word at a time instead of a syllable at a time.
Counting the two together would have looked like a bad splitter.

The true split is among the candidates 100.00% of the time and is the
only candidate 17.08% of the time, at a mean of 5.23 candidates per word,
so longest-first is a choice among real rivals rather than the only
reading going. It comes back whole slightly *more* often than it finds
the boundary, because two of the variant spellings read the same either
way.

The 0.81% of boundaries missed are one mechanism. Wade-Giles ends
syllables in -n and -ng and begins them with vowels and with n-, so
`i-ti-hu-na` run together as `itihuna` comes back `i-ti-hun-a`. Of 3,317
misses, 53.39% swallow a syllable beginning with n- and 36.72% one
beginning with a vowel. Pinyin is spared most of this by spelling a
zero-initial i- as `yi-`; Wade-Giles writes 一 as `i`, and 960 of the
misses — 28.94% — are a swallowed 一.

**And `Chungking` is not Wade-Giles.** The example this item was written
around, through two phases, is Postal Romanisation — and so are
`Tsingtao`, `Peking`, `Nanking` and `Canton`. `king`, `tsing`, `pe`,
`can` and `ton` are not Wade-Giles syllables at all; 重慶 in Wade-Giles is
`chʻung²-chʻing⁴` and 青島 is `chʻing¹-tao³`. The splitter returns
undefined for every one of them, which is the honest answer rather than a
gap, and the docs say so where the name used to be. `Mao Tse-tung`,
`Taipei` and `Kuomintang` really are Wade-Giles and are the cases this
handles. Checking cost one line against the inventory and changed what
the feature is for.

**The syllabic nasals are barred from a split**, and that bar is measured
rather than assumed. 嗯 `ng`, 呣 `m`, 唔 `n`, 噷 `hm` and 哼 `hng` are
syllables and read as such on their own — but not one of the 411,956
multi-syllable words contains one anywhere, first or otherwise. Without
the bar `ng` lets any run ending in -ng come apart, and `shung` — regular
Wade-Giles for a syllable Mandarin does not have, and the thing the index
exists to refuse — came back as `shu` + `ng`. Barring them costs nothing
that can be measured and moved every figure above up by a few hundredths.

Two smaller things:

- **A hyphen is a boundary except in `-êrh`**, which is part of a
  spelling: 花儿 huār is `hua-êrh` and stays one syllable, because the
  segmenter is offered the hyphens rather than cutting on them first and
  the longer head wins.
- **A tone digit ends a syllable**, so `pei³ching¹` splits without any
  rule about it — the digit is simply part of a head that reads.

Plus `transcribe --from wade-giles` learning whole words. A syllable
still gets every candidate, because `chu` stands for four and all four
fit on the screen; a word gets one row, because `maotsetung` splits five
ways before any of its syllables has been chosen. And its columns are a
floor now rather than a width — `mao-tsʻê-tung` is thirteen characters in
a column sized for `chʻü¹`, which is the third time in this repo a fixed
column width has gone stale. Only the cell that does not fit widens its
own column, so a single syllable is laid out exactly as before and no
guarded example moved.

`pnpm accuracy` and `pnpm polyphones` unmoved at 96.8% exact and 89.04%;
coverage holds at 100% statements, lines and functions.

## Checks

- `pnpm check` green — fmt, lint, fta, build, typecheck, tests with coverage.
- Coverage 100% statements, lines and functions; branches 96.34% against a 95%
  threshold. 1,165 tests over 67 files.
- `pnpm accuracy` and `pnpm polyphones` unmoved: 96.8% exact, 89.04% on CPP's
  20,139 polyphones.
- The corpus figures are produced by `pnpm romanization`, which grew a section
  for them, on the same footing as the 52.07% and 79.05% already on that page —
  the phrase corpus is fetched rather than committed, so those figures are
  attributed to the harness rather than asserted in a test, as the existing ones
  are.
- What *is* asserted: every example on the docs page, that the five Postal
  Romanisation names are refused and the three Wade-Giles ones are not, the
  syllabic-nasal bar, and that every pair of inventory syllables written solid
  splits except the nine a nasal is part of.

## Deliberately not done

- **Every candidate split.** `splitWadeGiles` returns one, as `splitSyllables`
  does. Handing back 5.23 splits with four candidates under each syllable is not
  an answer to give anybody, and the first-candidate rule is the one this module
  already measures.
- **儿化 written without its hyphen.** `hua-êrh` is 花儿 huār; `huaerh` splits as
  `hua` + `erh` and reads `huā ér`, because the suffix is keyed with its hyphen.
  Making the hyphen a droppable mark would change what `readWadeGilesLoosely`
  means, which is measured behaviour.
- **Postal Romanisation.** Not a system so much as a list, and not derivable
  from any of this — now stated on the docs page next to the names that prompted
  it.
- **hanzi → Wade-Giles end to end**, which is the other half of what Phase 6 had
  left. The undecided part is the orthography rather than the mapping: 正词法's
  word spacing is a pinyin standard and Wade-Giles hyphenates instead. Next PR.

author: claude[bot]
body:
## Description

Binds Melody's expression system to the authored expression catalog, so "she reads as a competitive gamer" becomes a measurement rather than an intention.

Three commits:

**1. Character template, MetaHuman backend, broken-file fix** (`080bc12dd`)

**2. Calibrate the Live2D backend against the authored expression set** (`ba7230a7c`)

The backend's parameter ranges were inferred from "typical Cubism range" rather than measured. Vendoring the 12 authored `.exp3.json` files makes the real envelope checkable, and checking it found four places the binding could not reach an authored pose:

- Head angles were 5x too large (`ParamAngleZ` drove +/-30 degrees; the authored set never exceeds 8). Overdriving here does not read as a bug, it reads as a deliberate bad art choice.
- `ParamAngleZ` was then scaled 6.0 but clamped at 8.0, so WONDER_02's authored +8 stayed unreachable.
- Eye openness bottomed at 0.40, so JOY_05 "Blissful" (0.15) could not be expressed at all.
- `ParamBrowLAngle`/`RAngle` were absent. SADNESS_01 pairs a *raised* brow (+0.15) with a *negative* angle (-0.30) - the oblique sad brow - so angle cannot be derived from raise.

**3. Bind the expression register to the authored catalog** (`a2de5d81d`)

The analysis documents name a rule the module was not following: "Competitive or game-like interaction" triggers the PUNK register, defined by asymmetry and a raised chin. Checking against that ground truth found three defects in shipped code:

- **AU17 was driven by `JawTension` alone.** Chin raise means defiance in the catalog, so the only way to lift the chin was to be *struggling* - a losing character asserted and a winning one never did.
- **Asymmetry was scaled by `Ease`**, so the harder the fight the more symmetric (and more synthetic) her face became, exactly when that costs the most.
- **`ComboFlow` was read and dropped.** It still counted toward signal coverage, and so toward the trust that unlocks expressiveness, while informing no part of the pose - a channel buying amplitude without paying for it.

`HeadTilt` is now signed; the authored set tilts both ways, so an unsigned magnitude could only ever produce half of it.

`AuthoredExpressionSet.h` places the named expressions in pose space. Two things keep it a measurement rather than a restatement of intent: prototype values are transcribed from the analysis documents and never tuned to make a test pass, and each prototype declares *which* channels the catalog actually pins down. Reading catalog silences as hard zeroes had made the JOY prototypes perfectly symmetric by omission, so the binding's deliberate non-synthetic asymmetry floor looked like evidence of a smirk.

`StandaloneExpressionRegister` asks for **reachability** rather than classification. "A winning Melody must classify as PUNK" would encode a guess and could be satisfied by nudging prototypes. Sweeping the signal x persona space and requiring every in-scope expression to be nearest to *some* reachable pose is objective - and it found a real gap:

| expression | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| PUNK_01 Confident Smirk | 29 / 1.5M | 8,617 |
| PUNK_02 Mischievous Grin | 45 / 1.5M | 23,907 |
| PUNK_05 Knowing Superiority | never nearest | 2,694 |
| JOY_06 Playful Grin | never nearest | 19,884 |

Both smirks sit at asymmetry 0.67 while the binding capped near 0.41. Melody could be defiant but could not smirk.

JOY_05 "Blissful" stays unreachable and is *declared* so - its triggers are transcendence and surrender, which no competence signal carries. The harness asserts the exclusion rather than tolerating a hole.

The sweep also exposed a scope limit in `StandaloneLive2DCoverage`, now recorded there: it sweeps the pose space, so it proves the *backend* can reach the authored values, not that the *system* can.

### Verification

All 9 standalone harnesses pass (`DeepTreeEcho/Tests/run_all.sh`). `StandaloneExpressionRegister` compiles the real binding rather than mirroring it, so its rules cannot drift from the rules that ship.

body:
## Intent

Fixes #2558 (GitHub-only issue; no Linear counterpart exists for it).

On iOS Safari (web/PWA), Shift+Enter in the chat composer submits the message instead of inserting a newline. This worked on 1.16.3 and regressed in 1.17.0/1.17.1 — the release range that shipped the CodeMirror composer migration (#2419).

Root cause: CodeMirror defers Enter on iOS (and Chrome Android): the real keydown never runs the composer's keymaps; the browser's native newline goes through, and the keymaps then run against a synthetic keydown that `dispatchKey` builds from the key name alone — carrying **no modifier keys**. The composer's `handleKeyDown` therefore saw the deferred Shift+Enter as a plain Enter (`key === 'Enter'`, `shiftKey === false`), and on devices where the desktop layout applies (`isMobile === false` — e.g. iPad Safari/PWA above 768px), the Enter branch `(!isMobile || e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey)` fired and submitted the message. On a textarea (1.16.3) the not-prevented Shift+Enter produced a native newline, so the loss never mattered.

Fix: record the real Enter keydown's shift state on the CodeMirror view's contentDOM (registered after CodeMirror's own listener, so it runs after the deferral decision but before the deferred dispatch) and restore `shiftKey` onto the synthetic event before the caller's `onKeyDown` policy runs. Shift+Enter now reaches the same `insertNewlineAndIndent` path plain Enter already used on iOS — a single newline. Plain Enter behavior is unchanged on every runtime: it still takes the identical deferred path it took before.

## Non-goals

- No change to what plain Enter does on any runtime (iPhone: newline; desktop-layout iPad: send; desktop: send). The reporter's regression is specifically Shift+Enter.
- No change to Backspace/Delete deferral, IME composition handling, or the `QuestionCard` textarea (a plain `<textarea>` — not CodeMirror — so its Shift+Enter already yields a native newline on iOS).

## Affected surfaces

- `packages/ui` — `components/chat/composer/editor/ComposerEditor.tsx` (the CodeMirror wrapper). The only consumer is `ChatInput.tsx`, which keeps its send policy untouched: it just sees `event.shiftKey === true` again for the deferred Shift+Enter.
- Runtimes: mobile web/PWA (Safari iOS — the reported surface; also Chrome Android, which uses the same `dispatchKey` deferral for Enter), Capacitor iOS/Android shells, desktop web, VS Code, Electron. The change is additive for every runtime: the ref is only consulted for CodeMirror `synthetic` keydown events (`keydown` events the library itself stamps), and `shiftKey` is only patched when the recorded real Enter carried Shift. Desktop never produces synthetic Enters, so its path is byte-for-byte the previous one.
- No persisted data, no exports, no new dependencies.

## Repository guidance

| Guidance | Why it applies | How the change complies |
|---|---|---|
| AGENTS.md — keep bridges thin, policy in owning modules | `ChatInput.tsx` owns the Enter/send policy; `ComposerEditor` owns CodeMirror internals | The CodeMirror synthetic-event quirk is contained in `ComposerEditor`; the caller's `onKeyDown` contract is unchanged |
| `packages/ui/src/components/chat/composer/DOCUMENTATION.md` | Defines module ownership ("`ChatInput.tsx` is the orchestrator… should not grow logic that belongs to [the modules]") and test limits ("keyboard behavior… not covered by tests, verified by hand") | Fix lives in `editor/` (the CodeMirror wrapper layer); no unit test was added because the package has no DOM test environment and this path is explicitly hand-verified per the docs |
| `openchamber-change-discipline` skill | Any OpenChamber source change | Smallest complete change: one internal helper + a listener + a shift restore in the existing `interceptKeys` binding; no refactors, no new deps, no export changes |
| `theme-system` skill (loaded per task) | Task required loading it | No UI/styling change; no theme tokens involved |

## Validation

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `bun run type-check:ui` (packages/ui) | Passed — `tsc --noEmit` clean |
| `bun run lint:ui` (packages/ui) | Passed — eslint clean |
| `bun test packages/ui/src/components/chat/composer/` | 277 pass, 0 fail (15 files) |
| `bun run dead-code` | Not run — no files/exports/entrypoints added, deleted, or renamed (one internal function added) |

Not verified (impossible in this environment): actual iOS Safari/iPad hardware-keyboard behavior. The composer documentation states keyboard behavior is verified by hand, not by tests. The mechanism was traced statically through the installed `@codemirror/view` 6.10.2 source: `InputState.keydown` defers iOS Enter (`PendingKeys`/`flushIOSKey`) and Chrome Android Enter (`delayAndroidKey`), both re-dispatching through `dispatchKey`, which builds `new KeyboardEvent("keydown", { key, code, keyCode, which })` with no modifier keys and stamps `synthetic = true`; `buildKeymap` folds the `any` binding into the `Enter` binding's run chain, so the deferred event reaches `onKeyDown` with `shiftKey === false`.

Expected behavior after the fix, to be confirmed on device: iOS Safari (iPhone and iPad/PWA) — Shift+Enter inserts a newline in the composer without sending; plain Enter behaves exactly as before (newline on iPhone, send on desktop-layout iPad); hardware-keyboard Enter follows the same paths.

## Visual evidence

No screenshots/recordings: this environment has no iOS simulator or browser, and the composer documentation notes keyboard behavior must be hand-verified on hardware. The change has no rendering effect — it only alters which key-handling branch a keydown takes.

## Risks and failure behavior

- **Deferred-Enter pairing**: each synthetic Enter is preceded by its own real Enter keydown (the pending state is set only by a real event and cleared by the flush), so the recorded shift state always belongs to the matching press. A stale ref cannot be consulted by a synthetic event that has no corresponding real one.
- **Kept-alive views** (`viewStore`): the recording listener lives on the view's `contentDOM` and the `interceptKeys` closure was created with the same ref, so both survive remounts and stay in sync.
- **CodeMirror version drift**: the fix depends on two documented internals — the `synthetic` expando on deferred events and the modifier loss in `dispatchKey`. If a future CodeMirror version preserves modifiers, the recorded state and the event agree and behavior is unchanged (the patch only applies when the synthetic event is missing the shift it really had).
- **Failure behavior**: the deferred Enter follows the identical pre-existing path (native newline + keymap run); the fix only changes which branch `onKeyDown` takes for Shift+Enter. No cleanup, rollback, or data concerns — the composer state machine, submit assembly, and message queue are untouched.

MAO는 Electron GUI와 headless CLI가 동일한 AI 주도 GitHub 워크플로우(`issue -> PR -> review -> merge`)를 공유합니다. 에이전트가 현재 코드의 경계, 실제 외부 부작용, 검증 명령을 매번 재발견하지 않도록 코드 근거의 공통 지침이 필요합니다.

이 PR은 아키텍처·보안·역할 규칙과 실행 절차를 분리한 SSOT를 만들고, Claude·Codex·Antigravity가 그 SSOT만 참조하도록 구성합니다. 비즈니스 로직과 제품 코드는 변경하지 않습니다.

## 🛠️ 추가/수정된 파일 (What changed)

- `AGENTS.md`: 제품 목적, `core/`·`electron/`·`cli/`·`src/` 의존 경계, workflow/maker-checker 불변조건, 보안 규칙, Architect/Implementer/Reviewer/Maintainer 역할을 정의합니다.
- `SKILL.md`: YAML frontmatter와 함께 설치, 빌드, 테스트, CLI, PR 리뷰·게시, 패키징 절차와 변경 유형별 검증 매트릭스를 제공합니다.
- `CLAUDE.md`: `@AGENTS.md`, `@SKILL.md`만 import하는 Claude 진입점입니다.
- `.agents/rules/mao-ssot.md`: 현재 Antigravity workspace rule 경로에서 루트 SSOT를 참조합니다.
- `.agents/skills/mao-development/SKILL.md`: Codex/Antigravity가 발견할 수 있는 얇은 native skill adapter입니다.
- `.antigravity/rules`: 요청된 legacy 호환 경로를 유지하면서 활성 rule과 루트 SSOT만 연결합니다.

관심사는 다음처럼 분리했습니다.

- Architecture, security, invariants, roles → `AGENTS.md`
- Commands, validation, repeatable workflows → `SKILL.md`
- Tool-specific discovery/import → thin adapter files

## 💡 향후 AI 에이전트 활용 가이드 (How to use)

1. 모든 작업 시작 시 `AGENTS.md`와 `SKILL.md`를 먼저 읽습니다.

author: victorigualada
body:
## Why

Run [30995358308](https://github.com/victorigualada/openrouter-benchmarks/actions/runs/30995358308) lost **all 1,075 tests across all four datasets**, every one at config-entry setup:

```
INFO openai._base_client: Retrying request to /models in 0.48s
INFO homeassistant.config_entries: Config entry 'Mock Title' for open_router
     integration not ready yet: Connection error.; Retrying in 5 seconds
```

Not a single request ever reached the model. The real cause is hidden: `openai._base_client` flattens any non-timeout exception into `APIConnectionError("Connection error.")`, and `open_router.async_setup_entry` converts that into `ConfigEntryNotReady`.

Reproduced locally on the exact CI stack (HA 2026.7.4, phcc 0.13.348, openai 2.53.0, python-open-router 0.3.3). Unwrapping `__cause__` gives:

```
openai.APIConnectionError: Connection error.
  <- RuntimeError: DNS resolution disabled in tests
  <- ValueError: b'openrouter.ai' does not appear to be an IPv4 or IPv6 address
```

`pytest_homeassistant_custom_component/plugins.py:224` locks the network down **twice** on every test:

1. `socket.getaddrinfo` / `gethostbyname` / `gethostbyname_ex` patched to reject any host that isn't an IP literal.
2. `pytest_socket.socket_allow_hosts(["127.0.0.1"])` + `disable_socket()`, which rejects the `connect()` even once a name resolves.

The datasets repo's `mock_allow_sockets` fixture undoes only (2). I hit (2) myself mid-fix: with DNS repaired, connects still failed against the localhost allowlist.

**This landed in HA 2026.5.0** — `tests/conftest.py` has no such guard in 2026.1.1 / 2026.2.3 / 2026.3.0 / 2026.4.0, and has it from 2026.5.0 onward. The last green benchmarks were February on HA 2026.2.x, so every run since has been broken for this reason, independent of model.

## What changed

`script/allow_real_dns.py`, a pytest plugin that lifts both layers, injected into the collect and metrics steps via `PYTHONPATH` + `PYTEST_ADDOPTS`. It teardown-restores the harness patches afterwards.

It is injected rather than committed into the datasets checkout because `setup` runs `gh repo sync` from upstream on every run, which would discard any patch there.

Two constraints, both found by testing and both recorded in the module docstring:

- **It cannot be a fixture.** The config entry is created in the `conversation_agent_config_entry` fixture, so a fixture-based fix races it.
- **The hook must not be `trylast`.** That moves it after `_pytest.runner.pytest_runtest_setup`, which is what runs the fixtures — the patch then lands after the failure. Plain registration order puts it after phcc (loaded via its `pytest11` entry point) and before the runner.

## Testing

Against the real dependency set, dummy API key throughout (`/api/v1/models` is public, so a reachable socket returns 200):

| case | result |
|---|---|
| control, outside pytest | OK — request completed |
| in pytest, no fixture | `DNS resolution disabled in tests` |
| in pytest, `socket_enabled` | `DNS resolution disabled in tests` |
| in pytest, datasets' `mock_allow_sockets` | `DNS resolution disabled in tests` |
| in pytest, HA's `get_async_client(hass)` (real integration path) | `DNS resolution disabled in tests` |
| **with this plugin** | **OK — request completed** |

Also verified: the network call succeeds when made from a *fixture* (as in CI) and not only from a test body; the fix holds with phcc loading solely through its entry point, matching the datasets repo; it holds under `pytest-random-order`; and the hooks install the real resolver then restore the sandbox, asserted directly.

## Note

A matching fix belongs upstream in `allenporter/home-assistant-datasets` — this breaks every live-LLM model there, not just ours. Filing that separately; this keeps us unblocked meanwhile.

author: paolodelcasale
body:
## Incident

A second authenticated Orca-hosted Pi smoke test reached the corrected `worker-start --terminal` seam but failed one member of a two-worker batch with:

```text
agent_unconfigured: Terminal term_389... is not running a recognized agent
```

Its concurrently launched sibling was recognized and attached successfully. The Pi TUI readiness signal can therefore precede Orca agent-hook registration.

The partial-batch rollback then stopped the successful sibling. Because exactly routed terminals are created before `worker-start`, Orca classifies them as external/reused; the stopped Dispatch later rejected `worker-release` with `dispatch_inactive`, leaving `minions_close` blocked.

## Fix

- retry only transient `agent_unconfigured` results for a bounded 10-second registration window
- preserve all other worker-start failures and uncertain-mutation reconciliation unchanged
- when `worker-release` reports a retained external terminal, close the exact terminal recorded by Minions
- treat stopped/inactive or already-gone external terminals as idempotent cleanup success
- update ADR and README lifecycle documentation

## Regression evidence

Real reproduction: `run_485a5d99f11c`, Dispatch `ctx_61e969c364ec` on Orca 1.4.169.

Automated validation:

- focused Orca runtime suite covers delayed hook registration, retained external cleanup, inactive stopped cleanup, legacy low-level recovery, and uncertain worker-start recovery
- full Pi suite: 56/56 passed

Achter Stapel: wissenschaftliche Bibliotheken, Forschungsdateninfrastruktur, Messnetze, Citizen Science, Sport, Kultur und Erwachsenenbildung.

## Bei Infrastruktur trägt ein anderes Argument

Ein guter Teil dieses Stapels ist Forschungsinfrastruktur — NFDI-Konsortien, Terminologie-Services, PID-Register, Lizenzmetadaten, SOEP-Codebuch. Dort wäre „kein Personenbezug" zwar richtig, aber nebensächlich. **Offenheit ist dort Funktionsbedingung, nicht Zugeständnis:**

- Ein Terminologie-Service nützt nur, wenn alle Fachcommunities ihn verwenden können.
- Lizenzangaben müssen sichtbar sein, damit Forschungsdaten überhaupt nachnutzbar sind.
- Ohne Codebuch wäre ein Panel nicht auswertbar — die Dokumentation beschreibt die Erhebungsinstrumente, nicht die Antworten der Befragten.

Bei den Messnetzen (Spurengase, Geomagnetik, Seismologie, kosmische Strahlung) steht entsprechend, dass ihr Wert erst aus dem internationalen Vergleich entsteht.

## Ein Fall, wo die Beschreibung die Begründung liefert

`antidoping-kontrollquote-sportart` sagt selbst: „Enthält Kontrollarten, nicht aber Ergebnisse auf Individualebene." Das ist die Begründung — sie musste nur aus der Beschreibung in das dafür vorgesehene Feld.

author: thelivinsine
body:
D22 left this open on the grounds that Streamlit does not execute scripts inside markdown. It does not, but `st.components.v1.html` does, and it is same-origin with the page hosting it, so this needs no component package and no new dependency.

`components.scrollspy()` returns the script; `app.py` renders it last, in a zero-height iframe, because it reads the sections it highlights.

## Written as an addition, not a dependency

- The reach into the parent document is inside a `try/catch` that returns, so a future Streamlit that sandboxes the iframe costs the nav its highlight and nothing else. The nav's resting state stays legible on its own.
- It stores no DOM node. Streamlit replaces nodes on rerun, so the handler re-queries links and sections each frame instead of holding references that would point at detached elements.
- The current section is marked in **three channels** (green underline, darker label, filled number), so it survives greyscale and a colour-blind reader. Consistent with the rule that hue never carries meaning alone.
- The scroll listener is in the capture phase on the document, because scroll events do not bubble and the page scrolls inside Streamlit's main element rather than the window.
- On a narrow screen the strip's `scrollLeft` is set directly to bring the marked link into view. `scrollIntoView` would also scroll the page and fight the reader.

## Also in here

A defect found while checking this at 390px: Streamlit 1.60 keeps `st.columns` side by side at every width, so the export checklist rendered about one word per line on a phone. Columns now wrap to full width below 640px.

## Verified

- In the browser at 1280px and 390px: the highlight tracks scrolling through all five sections, follows a click on the nav, and at 390px the strip scrolls the marked link into view.
- 154 tests green (was 151). Three new ones pin what a browser cannot check cheaply: the nav and the highlight are built from one list, the failure path returns, and nothing is cached.
- Zero horizontal page scroll at 375, 640, 768 and 1440.

author: silasfelinus
body:
## Incident root cause

Production Vercel functions were correctly clamped to `connectionLimit=2`, `minimumIdle=0`, and `idleTimeout=15`, but every Prisma query then timed out with:

```text
pool timeout: failed to retrieve a connection from pool after 10000ms
(pool connections: active=0 idle=0 limit=2)
```

The network, TLS, ProxySQL, credentials, migrations, and MariaDB capacity are healthy. The failure is inside the private MariaDB connector bundled by `@prisma/adapter-mariadb` 7.9.1:

- the adapter installs `mariadb 3.4.5`
- that pool implementation only creates connections while `idleConnections < minimumIdle`
- with `minimumIdle=0`, it never creates the first connection for a queued request
- the repository already installs top-level `mariadb 3.5.3`, whose pool creates a connection when requests are waiting

## Change

- add an idempotent build guard that removes only the adapter's known-broken private connector when it is older than 3.5.0
- verify the adapter then resolves to a connector that supports on-demand growth with `minimumIdle=0`
- run the guard before Prisma generation, migrations, maintenance tasks, and Nuxt bundling in Vercel
- run the same guard immediately after `npm ci` in TypeScript CI

## Why this shape

A package override would require regenerating the lockfile and changes Prisma's dependency graph globally. This guard is narrower: it modifies only installed `node_modules`, preserves the safe zero-idle serverless profile, is repeatable on cached Vercel installs, and fails loudly if the fixed top-level connector disappears.

## Production verification required

After merge and production deployment:

- `/api/health/database` must return HTTP 200
- runtime logs must stop reporting `active=0 idle=0 limit=2`
- ProxySQL frontend usage must remain bounded rather than returning to 200/200
- rerun the idempotent Achievement catalog and artwork maintenance that yielded during the incident

author: edwh
body:
Acts on moderator feedback about the standard-message editor (the `<editthis>` /
`<optional>` directives), plus the member-facing end of it.

## The send that looked like it had hung

Hitting **Send** with an `<editthis>` box unfilled or an `<optional>` section
undecided set a warning and returned - without calling the `SpinButton`
callback. The button then span for 20 seconds until SpinButton's
"callback forgotten" timeout, which also fired a Sentry report each time. Two
moderators independently reported this as the send hanging, with no idea what
was wrong.

The callback is now returned, so the button stops. The message says **nothing
has been sent yet** and what is left to do, the outstanding boxes are outlined
in red, the first is scrolled to, and both the outlines and the wording update
as each one is dealt with.

![send refused](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Freegle/Iznik/pr-assets/stdmsg-mod-feedback/02-send-refused.png)

## Optional sections

- **Keep was final.** Only a Remove could be undone. Both are reversible now.
- **The wording was fixed text.** It is an editable box, so an optional bit can
  be reworded as well as taken or left.

## Paragraph spacing

The line break between two blocks rendered as an empty full-height textarea. It
read as a field someone had forgotten to fill in, and gave no clue that it held
the paragraph spacing - so a message built from a template written with single
line breaks arrived with its paragraphs run together, and there was no obvious
way to fix it.

It is now a toggle saying whether there is a blank line there, with one click to
add or remove one. A separator of only spaces is left alone: that is inline
wording, not paragraph spacing.

| Editor as opened | After the decisions, with blank lines added |
|---|---|
| ![editor](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Freegle/Iznik/pr-assets/stdmsg-mod-feedback/01-editor.png) | ![decided](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Freegle/Iznik/pr-assets/stdmsg-mod-feedback/03-decided.png) |

## Boxes that looked empty

`AutoHeightTextarea` only started its row-growth check from the `currentValue`
watcher, which never fires for the value the component was mounted with. So
every pre-filled box - the standard-message template being the case that
matters - sat at its minimum rows with a scrollbar, and moderators reported the
wording looking like it was not there at all. It now grows to fit on mount, in
one bounded pass.

This is a shared component. Boxes that start empty (chat, ChitChat) are
unaffected: the pass only runs when there is something to fit.

## Hold buttons

`variant()` returned `warning` for `Hold Message`, the same amber as the
rejects, so in an alphabetically sorted set of buttons the holds ran into that
block and got picked by mistake. Holding a post keeps it, so they are now green
like the leaves (`rgb(51, 136, 8)` against the rejects' `rgb(227, 141, 19)`);
the pause icon still distinguishes them from a plain leave.

## Clickable links in volunteer chat

Freegle-side chat deliberately does not linkify URLs, because a link from
another member could be a scam. A `User2Mod` chat is the conversation with your
own community's volunteers, so that reasoning does not apply - and it left the
`$editlink` in a standard message as dead text in the app, with no way to follow
it. Those chats now linkify. **Member-to-member chat is unchanged**, and a test
asserts it stays plain.

![volunteer chat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Freegle/Iznik/pr-assets/stdmsg-mod-feedback/04-volunteer-chat-link.png)

## Also

The fill-in instruction at the top of the editor is red again rather than muted
grey. It was set red deliberately in #752 and turned back to muted by a later
tidy-up; moderators were reading straight past the grey version.

## Not in this PR

There is a related request to have a standard message **also append a preset
note to the post itself**, so that everyone who sees the post knows the
situation and not just the poster. There is no combined reply-and-edit action
today and adding one is a design decision (a new standard-message field or
directive, plus the post-patch path), so it is deliberately left out rather than
bolted on here.

## Testing

- Full vitest suite green locally (14736), including new tests for the
  send-refused callback and highlighting, undoing a Keep, editing kept wording,
  the paragraph toggle, the space-only separator, mount-time growth, and the
  linkify split.
- Full Playwright suite run locally against rebuilt production containers:
  183/184, then the one failure (`test-browse.spec.js` search, a
  `net::ERR_ABORTED` on the signup homepage navigation, where the harness
  deliberately allows no retries) re-run and passing 6/6. That path is not
  touched by this change.
- Walked through by hand in ModTools against a seeded directive standard
  message, and in Freegle chat for both `User2Mod` and `User2User`.
- Moderator docs updated here too: `docs/moderators/02-moderating-posts.md`
  gains a section on the fill-in and optional parts, and now `covers:` the modal
  and the directive helpers.

The `pr-assets/stdmsg-mod-feedback` branch holding the screenshots is throwaway
and can be deleted after merge.

### ✨ PR Description
## 1. Problem & Context

Implements the third part of component CRUD operations for the MCP server (ED-24967). Exposes `manage-component` ability alongside existing `list-components`, enabling AI to create, update, rename, archive, and publish components with proper license gating and validation.

## 2. What Changed (Where)

- **components-repository.php**: Renamed `get_component_for_edit()` private method to public `get_for_edit()` to support external access patterns.
- **list-components-ability.php**: Refactored response structure—now returns top-level `capabilities` object; filters archived components from discovery list; only includes `is_archived` flag when explicitly requested by ID.
- **manage-component-ability.php**: New 615-line ability implementing all five actions (create/update/rename/archive/publish) with comprehensive input validation, circular dependency detection, atomic widget enforcement, and license-tier access control.
- **mcp/module.php**: Registered `Manage_Component_Ability` alongside `List_Components_Ability`; added `elementor/manage-component` to exposed abilities.
- **Tests & docs**: 814 test cases covering all actions, access gates, error paths; updated markdown docs with capability schema and component creation patterns.

## 3. How It Works

**Entry point**: `Manage_Component_Ability::execute()` routes on `action` field. Each handler (create/update/rename/archive/publish) checks `Components_Access_Controller` against license state—Pro required for mutations, expired license allows read/publish only.

**Create/update flow**: XML compilation via `Composition_Compiler` → element ID regeneration → circular dependency validation → atomic widget validation → repository persistence. Draft mode uses autosave without touching live document.

**Archive**: Bulk archive with partial failure reporting. **Publish**: Promotes autosave to main document.

**Response shape**: All success responses include `editor_url` + `llm_instructions` (components lack public permalinks). Capabilities now returned at response root level rather than per-component.

## 4. Risks

**License gating asymmetry**: Create/rename/archive blocked on core; update/publish allowed on expired. Risk: confusion if license lapses mid-workflow. Mitigation: error messages explicitly state license requirement; tests cover all tiers.

**Circular dependency detection**: Validates post-compilation before save. Edge case: self-referencing component XML accepted during create but fails on save. Acceptable since error is caught and reported with clear message.

**Autosave collision**: Draft mode creates autosave; race condition if two requests collide. Mitigation: WordPress autosave semantics handle this (last-write-wins), acceptable for this use case.

body:
This PR is a continuation of #1618 and introduces a "precise landing" feature, which allows the flight controller to temporarily adjust control gains for improved landing accuracy. Instead of a single straight-line descent, the Crazyflie hovers above the target with temporarily-tuned controller gains to let horizontal error settle out before the final descent.

This works well when there's accurate positioning data (Lighthouse or MoCap), enabling the Crazyflie to react to external disturbances. Good for successfully landing on Crazyflie Brushless charging docks.

Also, this PR adds new high-level CRTP commands for precise landing, with and without explicit yaw.

Currently, the PID and Mellinger controllers support this feature.

An older version of this PR has been tested in the [fishtank demo](https://github.com/bitcraze/crazyflie-firmware-experimental/tree/icra-2026) at ICRA 2026.
